events.credibility_reason: Its upper bound n conflicts with the same authors' later bound of 2n, and the n/2 family is known only from search excerpts.

events.ai_basis: This approach arose through discussions between the authors and ChatGPT 5.5 and 5.6. ... The classification also emerged from discussions between the authors and ChatGPT 5.6, after the authors directed attention to the implications between the possible assignments of the unspecified ranks. ... Building on this classification, the authors directed further discussions with ChatGPT 6 towards the remaining odd part sizes.

why: The statement asks whether any n-vertex graph needs more than floor(n/2) copies of each letter. Showing that a whole class of graphs never exceeds the threshold settles a restriction of that question, so it is a case. Mozhui-Krishna 2025 is a case: its bound 1+⌈m/2⌉ is at most floor(N/2) for every bipartite graph with N ≥ 4. The paper does not state that comparison; it is the researcher's arithmetic, and I checked it. Colbrook-Drysdale 2026 also settles the bipartite class (R ≤ ⌈N/4⌉), so it is a case too. It is a 17-day-old preprint, so unreviewed; the Lean build does not count as review. Its AI role is assisted, not generated: by the authors' account the approach, the obstruction classification and the odd-part argument came out of discussions with ChatGPT, but the humans directed those discussions and wrote the manuscript. The Hefty-Horn-Muir-Owens papers are scored none. Nothing readable in the record ties their lower bounds to general graphs or to floor(n/2); the 2026 excerpt covers only bipartite graphs and hypercubes. The pre-snapshot events are benchmarks and bounds, plus finite computations in Akgün et al., which are instances. None of them resolves the question.
doubts: The literal existential reading is trivially yes for small n: K1 has R = 1 > 0 and P3 has R = 2 > 1. No source frames the bullet that way, and I answered on the intended reading for large n. The Hefty-Horn-Muir-Owens lower bounds were not read. If either applies to general graphs and exceeds floor(n/2), that would answer the question yes, and the record cannot rule this out. The middle sentences of the Colbrook-Drysdale AI declaration were read through a fetch with length limits and were not confirmed verbatim. The Mozhui-Krishna 2025 case rests on the researcher's own comparison with floor(N/2), not on anything the paper states.
